core: Elasticity as a unit-free ratio of percentage changes measuring responsiveness of one variable to another
Price elasticity of demand: percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
The midpoint (arc) method for computing percentage changes so elasticity is direction-independent
Elastic (>1), inelastic (<1), unit elastic (=1), and the perfectly elastic/perfectly inelastic extremes
Determinants of price elasticity of demand: availability of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, share of budget, time horizon
The total revenue test: price up raises revenue if inelastic, lowers it if elastic, unchanged if unit elastic
A worked midpoint calculation with independently verified arithmetic
supporting: Cross-price elasticity of demand and its sign convention (substitutes vs complements)
Income elasticity of demand and its sign convention (normal vs inferior goods)
outOfScope: The demand and supply curves themselves, and shift-vs-movement (economics:foundations:demand, economics:foundations:supply)
Utility maximization and full consumer-choice theory (economics:foundations:consumer-choice)

claims.claim: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded of a good divided by the percentage change in its price; because both are percentages the measure is unit-free.

The midpoint (arc) method computes the percentage change in quantity as (Q2-Q1) divided by the average of Q1 and Q2 (times 100), and the percentage change in price as (P2-P1) divided by the average of P1 and P2 (times 100), giving the same elasticity in either direction.

Demand is elastic when the elasticity exceeds one (quantity changes by a larger percentage than price), inelastic when it is below one, and unit elastic when it equals one; perfectly inelastic demand has elasticity zero (vertical curve) and perfectly elastic demand has elasticity approaching infinity (horizontal curve).

In OpenStax's worked demand example (points B to A: Q from 2,800 to 3,000, P from $70 to $60), the midpoint method gives a quantity change of about 6.9%, a price change of about -15.4%, and an elasticity of about 0.45, classified as inelastic.

The total revenue test: because total revenue equals price times quantity, a price increase raises total revenue when demand is inelastic, lowers total revenue when demand is elastic, and leaves it unchanged when demand is unit elastic.

Price elasticity of demand is larger when close substitutes are available, when the good is a luxury rather than a necessity, when it takes a larger share of the budget, and when buyers have more time to adjust (elasticity is generally greater in the long run than the short run).

OpenStax cites illustrative estimated elasticities such as roughly 0.12 for housing (inelastic) and about 2.3 for restaurant meals (elastic), showing necessities tend to be inelastic and discretionary goods elastic.
Price elasticity of supply is the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

Cross-price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded of one good divided by the percentage change in the price of another; it is positive for substitutes and negative for complements.
Income elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income; it is positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods.

Independent worked example (constructed, not from a source): with price $4 to $5 and quantity 200 to 140, the midpoint method gives -35.3% quantity change, +22.2% price change, elasticity about 1.59 (elastic), and total revenue falls from $800 to $700 — consistent with the total revenue test.
